historical_timeline.summary: Born in the family Homestead in Amherst, Massachusetts.
Removed from Mount Holyoke Female Seminary for about a month with lung congestion and a cough.
Consumptive symptoms; takes a glycerine prescription for two years.
Consults a Boston ophthalmologist; treated while living in Cambridgeport from April to December.
Repeats the eye treatment and is apparently cured.
Nervous prostration after a death in her family; ill health continues to her death.
Dies in Amherst at 55; Bright's disease is entered on the death certificate.

claims.statement: Emily Dickinson was born on December 10, 1830, in the family Homestead on Main Street in Amherst, Massachusetts.
In the late winter of 1848 she was removed from Mount Holyoke Female Seminary for about a month because of lung congestion and a cough.

In 1851 she had symptoms then thought to be consumptive, consulted local and Boston doctors, and for two years took a glycerine prescription from a Boston tuberculosis specialist until the symptoms apparently subsided.
claims.clinical_interpretation: No diagnosis of tuberculosis is documented.

claims.statement: By her own account an eye affliction began in the fall of 1863; in February 1864 she consulted the Boston ophthalmologist Henry Willard Williams, lived in Cambridgeport from April to December 1864 to be near him for treatment, and repeated the treatment from April to October 1865, after which she was apparently cured.
The treatment required confinement in dim light, no reading, and writing only in pencil; she called her first stay in Cambridge eight months of Siberia.

No record of the eye diagnosis survives. Her main symptoms were sensitivity to light, aching eyes, and a restricted ability to do close work; iritis is considered the most likely explanation, and exotropia, a psychiatric cause, and hysterical hyperaesthesia of the retina have also been proposed.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretations; the 2012 review offers a further possibility rather than a conclusion.

claims.statement: Her withdrawal from normal social situations began in her mid-twenties; in later years she rarely went beyond the family Homestead and spoke with some visitors from behind a darkened door rather than face to face.
Scholars disagree whether her withdrawal was a deliberate artistic choice or had a medical origin, such as an anxiety condition.
claims.clinical_interpretation: No diagnosis is documented; labels such as agoraphobia or social anxiety are retrospective and disputed.

claims.statement: A 2013 review by Hirschhorn and Longsworth rejects a proposed diagnosis of epilepsy on scientific, clinical, and biographical grounds.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective debate; epilepsy is not used in the record.

claims.statement: Her death came after two and a half years of ill health that followed a death in her family in October 1883 and a consequent nervous prostration; she later had two blackouts and was confined to bed for the seven months before her death.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Nervous prostration is a nineteenth-century term, not a modern diagnosis.

claims.statement: Her letters mention severe headache and nausea, and her last illness ended in a coma with raspy, difficult breathing.
Her reclusiveness hampered her Amherst physician, because she would not admit him to her bedside to take a pulse.

She died in Amherst on May 15, 1886, aged 55; her physician entered Bright's disease as the cause on her death certificate, at the time a general diagnosis that included hypertensive symptoms as well as nephritis.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Bright's disease was a broad nineteenth-century label, not a specific modern kidney diagnosis.

claims.statement: Researchers have concluded that she died of heart failure caused by severe hypertension; no documentary evidence records the yellow pallor and odor associated with nephritis.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A retrospective interpretation; no blood pressure or kidney test from her lifetime exists.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Dickinson comes to the clinic for the first time in two years, on a quiet early appointment that combines this review, a kidney ultrasound, and her nephrology consultation so that she makes one trip. She started losartan 50 mg, atorvastatin 20 mg, and vitamin D3 three weeks ago and stopped naproxen. Her headaches are less frequent, about twice a week, and she takes acetaminophen for them. The morning nausea has eased. She has had no lightheadedness, cough, or muscle aches. Her home blood pressure averages 150/90 on her own upper-arm cuff, which read within 4 mmHg of the clinic device today. She has cut down on salted foods. She saw Dr. Adeyemi of nephrology this morning after the ultrasound.

referral.question: Stage G3a A2 chronic kidney disease with hypertension in a 54-year-old woman without diabetes. Please confirm the probable cause, advise whether further tests are needed, and advise on kidney-protective treatment and follow-up
referral.urgency: Routine, within four weeks; please see her on the same morning as her kidney ultrasound, since she travels with difficulty
referral.pertinent_history: Several months of morning headaches, nausea, and tiredness. Blood pressure 166/98 mmHg at today's home visit; she has never been treated for hypertension. She has taken over-the-counter naproxen several times a week for the headaches, stopped today. An urgent care visit fourteen months ago recorded an eGFR of 58 and a urine albumin-creatinine ratio of 190 mg/g, which were not followed up. Today: creatinine 1.20 mg/dL (eGFR 54), potassium 4.4 mmol/L, urine albumin-creatinine ratio 240 mg/g, urine red cells 1 per high-power field, hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, calcium 9.3 and phosphate 3.8 mg/dL, PTH 74 pg/mL, 25-hydroxyvitamin D 21 ng/mL, HbA1c 5.5 percent, LDL 134 mg/dL. KFRE 0.5 percent at 2 years and 1.6 percent at 5 years. ECG shows borderline voltage for left ventricular hypertrophy. Started today: losartan 50 mg, atorvastatin 20 mg, vitamin D3 1,000 units, and acetaminophen as needed. Never smoker; no alcohol. She has long wished to stay at home and asks for as few clinic trips as possible; video follow-up suits her
questions: Is hypertensive kidney disease the probable cause, or does she need further tests, such as serology or a kidney biopsy?
Should she take an SGLT2 inhibitor, given that she does not have diabetes?
What ARB dose and blood pressure target do you advise?
How should the raised PTH and low vitamin D be managed at this stage?
How often does she need nephrology follow-up, and can it be by video?

consultant_note.history: Ms. Dickinson is seen at the request of Dr. Hartwell for chronic kidney disease with albuminuria and newly treated hypertension. She has had morning headaches and nausea for several months and took naproxen for them until three weeks ago. A low eGFR and albuminuria were found fourteen months ago and not followed up, so the disease has lasted more than three months. She has no history of kidney disease in childhood, urinary infections, stones, rash, joint pain, or blood in the urine, and no diabetes. She takes no herbal remedies or proton pump inhibitors. She started losartan 50 mg three weeks ago
consultant_note.data_reviewed: The intake results, the ECG, today's metabolic panel and second urine albumin-creatinine ratio, home blood pressure readings, and this morning's kidney ultrasound

Soft; kidneys not palpable; no renal bruit

assessment.assessment: Confirmed: eGFR 51 to 58 for more than three months, with albuminuria of 240 and 262 mg/g on two samples. Long-standing untreated hypertension, borderline left ventricular hypertrophy on ECG, a bland urine without red cells, and normal-sized, mildly echogenic kidneys on ultrasound make hypertensive kidney disease the probable cause, possibly worsened by regular naproxen. With no hematuria, systemic features, nephrotic-range albuminuria, or rapid decline, a biopsy or glomerular serology is not needed now. KFRE is low, at 1.6 percent over 5 years
Above target on losartan 50 mg. Today's potassium of 4.6 mmol/L and creatinine of 1.26 mg/dL after three weeks allow the dose to be raised

assessment.display: Vitamin D deficiency with a mildly raised PTH
assessment.assessment: A PTH of 74 pg/mL at G3a with a low vitamin D is most likely from the vitamin D deficiency; calcium and phosphate are normal

recommendations: Raise losartan to 100 mg daily, the maximum dose, for A2 albuminuria

Start dapagliflozin 10 mg daily: KDIGO recommends an SGLT2 inhibitor in chronic kidney disease with eGFR of at least 20 and a urine albumin-creatinine ratio of at least 200 mg/g, with or without diabetes
Recheck potassium and creatinine 2 to 4 weeks after these changes; accept a creatinine rise of up to 30 percent
Aim for a standardized systolic pressure below 120 mmHg if tolerated; if home readings stay above target on the full ARB dose, add amlodipine
Repeat the urine albumin-creatinine ratio about three months after starting treatment to judge the response, then eGFR and urine albumin twice a year
Continue vitamin D3 1,000 units daily and recheck 25-hydroxyvitamin D, calcium, phosphate, and PTH in 6 to 12 months; no calcitriol
No NSAIDs; written sick-day rules for losartan and dapagliflozin during vomiting, diarrhea, or poor intake
Complete hepatitis B vaccination, as for all adults with chronic kidney disease
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Hartwell the same morning. Ms. Dickinson agrees with the plan and asked for it in writing
consultant_note.follow_up: Primary care leads, with home and video visits. Nephrology video review in about a year with the yearly tests, or sooner if eGFR falls by more than 20 percent and stays down, the urine albumin-creatinine ratio doubles, potassium is above 5.5 mmol/L, or the 5-year KFRE reaches 3 percent
